answer:
This vehicle's risk profile now centers on the software and ground-processes layer rather than new hardware failure modes: a small team, a single shared ground model, and long fault-response latencies create conditions where a subtle logic or validation gap — not a hardware break — is what has historically doomed similar spacecraft.

### 1. Fault protection responds in a way that is more hazardous than the fault itself
A postulated propulsion anomaly on Mars Observer would have put the spacecraft into a "stable" contingency mode that inhibited the radio amplifier and blocked autonomous recovery of downlink; ground commands were not sent until hours later because controllers trusted spacecraft autonomy, and by then batteries would likely have been depleted. Investigators found fault protection was built bottom-up with no RCS backup to reaction wheels and was never exercised on the flight unit before launch. [LLIS 343: Mars Observer Inappropriate Fault Protection Response Following Contingency Mode Entry](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/343); [LLIS 345: Mars Observer Attitude Control Fault Protection](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/345)

Check: confirm the enable/execute bounding logic and any safing response have been tested on flight (or flight-identical) hardware, that thrusters can stabilize the vehicle if wheels are unavailable, and that no terminal fault state can persist without autonomously restoring communications.

### 2. An uplinked software patch introduces an unreviewed side effect
Mars Observer's flight computer flexibility let controllers quickly uplink a script widening star-identification tolerance after inertial reference losses — but that patch had no detailed code walk-through, and it acted as a catalyst for three further inertial-reference-loss incidents via a pre-existing algorithm error inherited from another program. Recovery took days each time. [LLIS 310: Mars Observer Inertial Reference Loss](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/310)

Check: require a detailed code walk-through for every incremental flight-software patch, especially inherited modules, before uplink — not just regression testing against the ground model.

### 3. Sequences validated against a ground model that no longer matches onboard state
Galileo's star-scanner calibration sequence was tested and cleared on the testbed, but an in-flight mode change (gyros off instead of on) before execution was judged inconsequential; the mismatch between simulated and actual onboard state triggered a hardware-swap cascade and safing, with a three-week recovery just weeks before Venus encounter. [LLIS 288: Galileo Spacecraft Safing During Star Scanner Calibration](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/288)

Check: since sequences and builds share one ground model, re-verify any queued sequence against current onboard state whenever an anomaly or mode change has occurred since the last simulation run, before uplink.

### 4. Preloaded sequencing proves too rigid for real anomalies, and small-team/light-time constraints block timely correction
Voyager's operations concept assumed minimal real-time commanding, with most activity preloaded; flight experience showed real-time intervention was needed far more than planned, and the end-to-end system was cumbersome for it. [LLIS 270: Planning for Spacecraft Real-Time Commanding](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/270)

Check: with round-trip light time and a lean staff limiting response to tens of minutes, verify the real-time command path remains flexible and rehearsed, not an afterthought behind the sequencing engine.

This is a research aid drawn from historical records, not a substitute for a formal safety review.
